title: Irregular nouns and suffixes on verbs

objectives.can: Parse the common irregular nouns in their construct, plural and suffixed forms.
Identify a pronominal object suffix on a verb.

explanation.summary: A small group of very common nouns do not follow the ordinary patterns: their construct, plural and suffixed forms are built on changed stems. And a verb can carry a pronoun as a suffix, in which case the suffix is its object. Learning both makes many apparent mysteries in a verse disappear.

sections.heading: Irregular nouns: learn the set
body: Most Hebrew nouns follow a pattern, but fifteen of the commonest do not. Their construct form, their plural and their forms with suffixes use different stems from the absolute singular. The table gives the main forms of each as they stand in the Bible. Learn each noun as a set, because no rule predicts the plural of אִישׁ, 'man', which is אֲנָשִׁים, or the plural of אִשָּׁה, 'woman', which is נָשִׁים.

In the corpus a suffixed noun is labelled State=Cons: אָבִיו, 'his father', is the construct singular of אָב with the suffix 3rd masculine singular, because suffixes attach to the construct stem. The construct is often shorter than the absolute: אָב becomes אֲבִי, בֵּן becomes בֶּן in the singular and בְּנֵי in the plural.

sections.heading: Reading the irregular nouns in a verse
body: Genesis 2:24 contains four of them in one sentence: יַעֲזָב אִישׁ אֶת אָבִיו וְאֶת אִמּוֹ וְדָבַק בְּאִשְׁתּוֹ. The man (אִישׁ) leaves his father (אָבִיו) and his mother and clings to his wife (אִשְׁתּוֹ). The suffix -וֹ is 'his', and the stems אָבִי- and אִשְׁתּ- are the construct stems of אָב and אִשָּׁה.

Plurals need the same care. In Genesis 18:2 Abraham sees three אֲנָשִׁים, 'men': the plural of אִישׁ. In Exodus 12:27 the houses are בָּתֵּי, the plural construct of בַּיִת, 'the houses of the Israelites', and בָּתֵּינוּ is the same with the suffix 1st plural, 'our houses'. Where an ordinary plural would end in -ִים, these nouns often change the vowel under the first consonant or double a consonant: בָּתִּים with a doubled ת.

Two of the nouns have no singular in ordinary use. מַיִם, 'water', and שָׁמַיִם, 'heavens', are plural in form. In Genesis 1:8 God calls the expanse שָׁמָיִם. The construct forms מֵי and שְׁמֵי drop the final syllable: you will meet them as 'the waters of' and 'the heavens of'.

sections.heading: A pronoun attached to a verb
body: A verb can carry a pronoun as a suffix. On a verb the suffix is the object: it is 'him', 'me', 'you', not 'his' or 'my'. In Exodus 3:13 Moses is to say אֱלֹהֵי אֲבוֹתֵיכֶם שְׁלָחַנִי אֲלֵיכֶם, 'the God of your fathers has sent me to you'. The verb שְׁלָחַנִי is the Qal qatal 3rd masculine singular of שָׁלַח with the suffix 1st singular: the subject is God, the object is 'me'. The subject is always in the verb itself; the suffix adds the object.

The suffixes are close to those on nouns, but they usually attach after a linking vowel. After a qatal the link is a short a-vowel (שְׁלָחַנִי); after a wayyiqtol, yiqtol or imperative a linking vowel -ֵ- or -ֶ- is common. The stem of the verb often loses a vowel when the suffix is added: compare שָׁלַח with the first syllable of שְׁלָחַנִי and the Piel qatal צִוָּה with צִוָּהוּ, 'he commanded him'.

sections.heading: The energic nun, and suffixes on infinitives and participles
body: Before the suffix 3rd masculine singular, and sometimes before others, a yiqtol often takes an extra נ with a dagesh: וְלֹא יִשְׁמְרֶנּוּ in Exodus 21:29, 'and he does not keep it in'. The ending -ֶנּוּ is the suffix -נוּ with an added nun, called the energic nun by grammarians. The extra נ does not belong to the root: do not mistake it for a first-nun or a final-nun root.

Suffixes also attach to infinitives and participles. On an infinitive the suffix is usually the subject: בְּנָגְפּוֹ in Exodus 12:27 is 'when he struck' (literally 'in his striking'). Its object follows as a separate word. On a participle the suffix is usually the object or a possessive, as in מְבָרְכֶיךָ, 'those who bless you', in Genesis 12:3. The corpus uses the same feature, Suffix, in all these cases, so read the construction before you decide who is the subject.

misunderstandings: On a verb the suffix is the object, not the subject and not a possessor. שְׁלָחַנִי means 'he sent me', not 'my sending'.
A plural noun does not have to end in -ִים. אִישׁ has the plural אֲנָשִׁים, and אִשָּׁה has נָשִׁים, which look like different words. Learn the irregular plurals as sets.
The נ before -וּ in forms like יִשְׁמְרֶנּוּ is not a root consonant. Take off the whole ending -ֶנּוּ and see what is left.
A suffixed noun is labelled construct in the corpus. That is correct: the suffix attaches to the construct stem, so State=Cons does not mean that the noun is in a construct chain with another noun.

deeper.heading: Why these nouns are irregular
body: Many of the irregular nouns are old, short words whose base forms had different shapes before the vowels of Hebrew settled. Grammarians describe several of them (אָב, אָח, פֶּה) as having a longer stem that appears when something is added. These accounts are reconstructions, and the practical rule for reading is to learn the forms that actually occur.
